On Figma Motion, my demo & review. 

This is one of those updates that clicked swiftly into my workflow. Like in my 3D pipeline, using this stick shift animation, I emphasize hardware feedback with motion from Figma Motion. 

Assets are animated in Fig Motion and loaded into Blender as video textures for mesh and material control. 

It's advantageous since it is built into an ubiquitous ecosystem. A lot of work these days start in Figma even for someone like me that works outside the tool frequently. 

Can't over-emphasize my appreciation for the schema used to introduce motion to nearly all properties. Reminds me of how motion works in Blender - with better complexity management. Better than introducing more menus for those. Ease curves iD between keyframes is also an improvement over existing systems. 

Having spent some time on the tool, here are updates I'll like to see to Figma Motion. These are based on my immediate needs as at the time of working on this demo:

• Using modifier keys (CMD, Shift, Ctrl) to jump / nudge across the timeline. E.g: holding down Shift key to make the playhead jump 100ms etc.

• Jump to previous or next keyframe.

• Better anchor point trails

• Renaming layers from the timeline as well.

• Editable custom bezier styles: after saving a style, I should be able to edit the curve - just as you can edit colour styles.

• Enable transform on the timeline. I should be able to flip or scale keyframes.

I hope to continue trying more ideas. Craft focused tools have had to take a backseat in recent times. Pleasing to see this come to light.

Something people don’t realize about learning motion design: the software is the easy part. Most people get stuck long before they open After Effects.

The real skill is learning to see motion before you make it. When you watch a well-made brand animation, your brain registers it as smooth and satisfying. 

But if you slow it down frame by frame, there are dozens of decisions in there: when something starts moving, how fast it accelerates, whether it eases in or snaps, how long it holds before the next thing happens.

None of that is accidental and until you can see those decisions, you can’t recreate them, and you definitely can’t make your own.

The exercise that actually builds that skill faster than any course: pick a piece of motion you love, watch it ten times, then try to build it from memory. Don’t reference it while you work, just try.

Your version will be wrong but that’s the point. The gap between what you made and what you were trying to make tells you exactly what you don’t understand yet. No tutorial teaches that as directly.

Once you can see decisions, the next thing to learn is timing. Timing is the thing that separates motion that feels satisfying from motion that just moves. A perfectly designed animation with slightly off timing feels wrong in a way most people can’t name but everyone can feel.

The fastest way to develop timing is to watch a lot of work across different styles and start noticing how each one handles the moment just before and just after movement. That’s where the feeling of your design lives.

Tools matter a lot less than most beginners think. Figma, After Effects, Cinema 4D, Cavalry, Rive are all just containers for decisions. The designer who understands motion will make good work in any of them. The one who doesn’t will make average work in all of them.

Learn to see first ,feel timing second, after then pick up the tools.

After playing around with @figma motion this weekend, there are 2 major shortcomings that I found:

1. No way to animate individual anchor points on a vector path. This means that there is no way to morph shapes/polygons. 

2. No way to proportionally stretch timelines of multiple elements. I had animation that was too fast. I wanted to extend the time of everything at once to make it all move slower. Can't do it.

If I'm wrong about these, please tell me.

As expected, it's far from great

But it's not completely useless

It can do simple slideshows, mass update keyframes, easing, etc

Good way to eliminate repetitive work

This is the prompt i used btw:

Showcase animation: move the group to reveal each child frame one at a time, centered in the viewport. Jump between frames in a non-sequential order so the camera feels like it's exploring, no row-by-row pattern. Use smooth, human-like panning: gentle ease-in out of rest, long deceleration into each stop (cubic bezier ~0.4, 0, 0.2, 1). Hold each frame briefly before moving on. At the end, pan back to the first frame so the animation loops seamlessly
